orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. It is August 1801, a week after the first meeting on the moor. Edgar Linton is now very close to death, and Thursday has come round again for Cathy's ride to meet Linton.

notes.g: The quick decline that now set in.

notes.t: emulated by the inroads of hours
notes.g: Matched by the damage now done in mere hours.
Gladly have kept fooled (about how ill he was).
notes.n: 'Fain' means gladly or willingly.

notes.g: On the day fixed for the weekly meeting with Linton.

notes.t: Her countenance grew wan with watching
notes.g: Her face grew pale and drawn from sitting up with him.
notes.m: 'Watching' here means staying awake through the night at a sickbed, not looking at something.
'Society' here means company, not the community or high society.

notes.g: A weakness that can be forgiven.
The girl placed in my care.
notes.n: A 'charge' is a person you are responsible for.

notes.g: Wait on your whims and play-acting.
notes.n: 'Affectations' are put-on behaviour meant to impress or get attention.

notes.g: Too low and worthless to deserve your anger.
notes.m: 'Mean' here means low and contemptible, not unkind.

notes.g: Give me only contempt instead (and keep your hatred for him).
Ready for you without your asking.
The stone in front of the fireplace; the fireside at home.

notes.n: The usual British word for a girl's or woman's dress.

notes.m: Not 'beautiful' or 'refined'. 'Exquisite' could mean keenly or sharply felt.

notes.t: my life is in your hands

notes.m: Not 'divert my attention'. 'Distract' meant to confuse or drive frantic.

notes.n: 'Ling' is the common heather that covers the moors.

notes.g: Calling out a greeting to me.
That he put on for nobody else.
The bed where he is dying.

notes.n: Nelly means death will end Edgar's suffering and, as she believes, reunite him with his wife.

notes.t: that lad yonder seems determined to beat me
notes.g: That boy over there seems set on beating me: Heathcliff fears Linton will die before Edgar.
notes.n: If Linton dies first, he never inherits the Grange, and Heathcliff cannot claim it through him (Chapters XX and XXI). That is why Heathcliff wants Edgar to 'be quick'.

notes.g: The puppy; a scornful word for a young man.
Cathy; Heathcliff uses her formal title.
His girlfriend; the girl he is courting.

notes.t: under the hands of a doctor

notes.g: Lie face down, like a beggar or slave.
A raised bank of grassy ground.
Her worries about obeying her father.
notes.n: 'Filial' means to do with a son or daughter's duty to a parent.

notes.g: You are very stubborn and unbending.

notes.t: pinch the baby and make it scream
notes.g: Hurt the child until he cries.
notes.n: Heathcliff mocks Nelly: must he torment Linton before she will take pity and help?

notes.g: Said sarcastically to the cowering Linton.

notes.n: 'Gripe' is an old form of 'grip'.

notes.g: Frightening him out of his wits.

notes.n: Houses with plague were shut up and avoided. Heathcliff means: don't be afraid to come in.

notes.t: I have a mind to be hospitable

notes.m: Not 'I began'. To 'start' was to flinch or jump with surprise.

notes.g: Hareton Earnshaw, Cathy's cousin on her mother's side, who works the farm at the Heights.
Probably the name of some meadows or pastures.
notes.n: 'Lea' or 'lee' is an old word for a meadow.

notes.g: A pleasure trip; a day out.

notes.t: laws are less strict and tastes less dainty
notes.g: Where the law is looser and people are less squeamish.
Slowly cutting them up while alive.
notes.n: Vivisection means cutting into a living animal, as some scientists did for research.

notes.t: the person from whom she inherited it
notes.n: Cathy has her mother's dark eyes and fiery boldness, and for a moment Heathcliff is reminded of her.

notes.g: Let go of the thing they were fighting over.

notes.t: ere she had well secured it
notes.g: Before she had properly got hold of it.
notes.n: 'Ere' means before.

notes.t: had she been able to fall
notes.g: If she hadn't been held on his knee (so she couldn't be knocked down).

notes.n: An old way of describing a dangerous fit of fury.
Reeds are thin waterside plants that shake in the slightest wind.

notes.t: I shall be your father, to-morrow
notes.n: He means the wedding he is planning. People often said 'father' for father-in-law.

notes.t: all the father you’ll have in a few days
notes.g: Heathcliff expects Edgar to die within days.
A long wooden bench with a high back, set by the fire.

notes.t: the correction had alighted on another
notes.g: The punishment had landed on someone else.

notes.n: The spleen was once thought to be the seat of anger and spite.

notes.t: your own naughty pet and mine

notes.g: Nelly's formal name for young Linton.
Truly locked in; well and truly imprisoned.

notes.n: A common punishment for children then.

notes.t: menaced with an awful visitation of wrath
notes.n: A 'visitation' was a punishment sent from above, as from God. Nelly uses the grand phrase for Heathcliff's rage.
A decoy is a fake or tame bird used to lure wild birds into a trap.

notes.t: we are to be married in the morning
notes.g: A wedding the very next morning.
notes.n: In England a quick wedding needed a marriage licence; otherwise banns had to be read in church on three Sundays. For anyone under 21, a licence needed a parent's or guardian's consent. Cathy is seventeen, and Edgar has not consented.

notes.t: he’s afraid of my dying if we wait
notes.g: Heathcliff wants the marriage to happen while Linton is still alive.
notes.n: Remember his boast that his son would be 'lord' of the Linton estates (Chapter XX).
In folklore, fairies stole a healthy baby and left a sickly fairy child, a 'changeling', in its place.

notes.g: Holding on fondly to the idea.

notes.n: 'Dastardly' means cowardly; 'puling' means whimpering like a baby.

notes.t: commenced the execution of her threat
relieve him from this cruel suspense
notes.g: Spare him this awful worry about where I am.
The persuasive words fear gives a coward.
Almost out of her mind with worry.
Get his selfish panic under control.

notes.t: pay her back her present tyrannies with a vigorous hand
notes.g: Pay her back for her bullying now, with force.
I'll take care of the rest.
Like a nervous dog slinking past someone it fears.
Planning to give it a cruel pinch.

notes.t: his neighbourhood revived a painful sensation
notes.g: Being near him brought back the pain.
notes.m: 'Neighbourhood' here means nearness, not the area where you live.

notes.g: Terribly afraid (a strong swear word then).
There are laws in this country to stop this.
I'd report him to the authorities.
notes.n: That is, to a magistrate.

notes.g: A serious crime punishable by hanging, with no way out.
notes.n: 'Benefit of clergy' was an old legal loophole that let many first offenders escape the death penalty (originally by proving they could read, like a clergyman). The worst felonies were excluded. Carrying off an heiress and forcing her to marry had long been one of these hanging crimes.

notes.t: fixing your residence under my roof
notes.g: Making sure you stay in my house.

notes.t: his happiest days were over when your days began
notes.g: His wife died when you were born.
notes.n: Cathy's mother died two hours after giving birth to her (Chapter XVI).

notes.g: Your main entertainment from now on.
Make up for what else you lose.

notes.t: His letters of advice and consolation entertained me vastly
notes.g: Edgar's letters to Linton amused me enormously.
notes.n: Heathcliff insisted on seeing every letter Edgar sent his son (Chapter XXV).

notes.t: recommended my jewel to be careful of his
notes.g: Urged my treasure (Linton) to take good care of his (Cathy).
notes.n: Heathcliff is mocking Edgar's fatherly language.

notes.t: their teeth be drawn and their claws pared
notes.g: They have their teeth pulled out and claws clipped, so they can't fight back.
A monster of legend that could kill with a look.
notes.n: A serpent said to hatch from a cock's egg. The Bible mentions it several times: 'out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice' (Isaiah 14:29). Nelly means Linton is his father's poisonous offspring.

notes.g: In a way that can never be undone.
Heathcliff is her uncle by marriage.
notes.n: He married her father's sister, Isabella.
An eft is a newt, a small, cold, damp creature like a lizard.

notes.g: Clinging to me and trying to win me over, like a dog.

notes.m: 'Dumb' here means unable or not allowed to speak, not stupid.

notes.t: he had his wits about him

notes.n: A lattice window has small panes set in a crisscross of lead strips.
'Chit' is a scornful word for a young girl.

notes.g: The trapdoor up into the attic.

notes.t: took her station by the lattice

notes.n: Hareton speaks broad Yorkshire.
'Prayers' here means requests, not prayers to God.

notes.g: Sullen, silent, and refusing to listen.

notes.t: moving his sense of justice or compassion
notes.g: Appealing to his fairness or pity.
